```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6,
                      fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
```

This vignette walks through the procedure of `hotcoldESF` on one simulated
dataset: the example shown in Figure 1 of the paper that introduces the method.
The data contain three clusters of points, an area with fewer points than expected
(a true cold spot), and an area with many points that are explained by a
covariate. A good method should find the clusters and the cold area, and should
**not** flag the covariate area, because its excess of points is explained by the
covariate.

```{r}
library(hotcoldESF)
```

## The data

`sim_thomas()` simulates points in a 1000 x 1000 window and counts them on a
20 x 20 grid. This is scenario K of the simulation study (strong version):

* three clusters of 200 points each (radius 100);
* a cold area of radius 150 that keeps only 20% of its points;
* 2000 points spread uniformly;
* 3000 points whose intensity follows an environmental covariate (a smooth bump).

```{r data}
set.seed(10)
s <- sim_thomas(k = 20, n_parents = 3, radius = 100, sons = 200,
                n_background = 2000, n_cov = 3000, min_dist = 300,
                n_cold = 1, cold_keep = 0.2)
str(s[c("Y", "Z", "A")])
```

The model receives two covariates: `env`, the value of the bump at the centre of
each cell, and `noise`, an irrelevant standard normal variable. `A` is the queen
contiguity matrix of the grid.

Two small helpers draw a map of the cells and the true clusters (dashed) and
cold area (dotted).

```{r helpers}
k <- s$k; side <- s$cell_side
draw_map <- function(v, cols, zlim = range(v), main = "") {
  image(seq(0, 1000, length.out = k + 1), seq(0, 1000, length.out = k + 1),
        matrix(v, k, k), col = cols, zlim = zlim, asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
        xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main, font.main = 1, cex.main = 0.9)
  th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(s$parents)))
    lines(s$parents[i, 1] + s$radius[i] * cos(th),
          s$parents[i, 2] + s$radius[i] * sin(th), lty = 2)
  ctr <- colMeans(s$centres[s$cold_cells, , drop = FALSE])
  lines(ctr[1] + 150 * cos(th), ctr[2] + 150 * sin(th), lty = 3)
  rect(0, 0, 1000, 1000, border = "grey60")
}
greens <- colorRampPalette(c("#f2f7ee", "#a8d08d", "#4d9a3a", "#1f5f1a"))(100)
diverging <- colorRampPalette(c("#184f95", "#6da7ec", "#f0efec", "#ec8a89", "#a32727"))(101)
```

```{r counts, fig.height = 3.6}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
plot(s$points, pch = 16, cex = 0.15, asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     xlim = c(0, 1000), ylim = c(0, 1000), main = "Points", font.main = 1, cex.main = 0.9)
draw_map(log1p(s$Y), greens, main = "log(1 + counts) per cell")
par(op)
```

The largest counts are in the covariate area (right). Ranking cells by their counts
would send resources there, although nothing beyond the covariate is going on.

## Running the procedure

`hot_cold_map()` runs the four steps of the method with its default settings:

1. regress \(y\), the standardised \(\log(1 + Y)\), on the covariates and test
   the residuals for spatial autocorrelation with Moran's I (exact moments);
2. estimate the spatial component \(\hat f\) by eigenvector spatial filtering
   (smooth eigenvectors of `A`, ridge penalty chosen by cross-validation);
3. compare each \(\hat f_i\) with its distribution under 999 permutations of the
   residuals: hot above the 95% quantile, cold below the 5% quantile;
4. group the hot (cold) cells into zones.

We keep the permuted fits (`keep_null = TRUE`) only to plot the band below.

```{r fit}
set.seed(17)
h <- hot_cold_map(s$Y, s$Z, s$A, keep_null = TRUE)
h
```

The test of Step 1 rejects (\(z_0\) is large), so the procedure continues.

## The spatial component

\(\hat f\) is the part of the log counts that the covariates do not explain and
that is shared by neighbouring cells. Positive values (red) have more points than
the covariates predict; negative values (blue) fewer.

```{r fhat, fig.height = 3.6}
zl <- max(abs(h$fhat)) * c(-1, 1)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
draw_map(log1p(s$Y), greens, main = "log(1 + counts)")
draw_map(h$fhat, diverging, zl, main = "spatial component f-hat")
par(op)
```

Once the covariate is accounted for, the covariate area disappears, while the
three clusters and the cold area remain.

## The permutation band

For each cell, the band is the range of values \(\hat f_i\) would take if the
residuals had no spatial structure. Here are the observed value and the band for
three cells: the cell with the largest \(\hat f\), the neutral cell with the
largest \(\hat f\), and the cell with the smallest \(\hat f\).

```{r band, fig.height = 3}
neutral <- which(h$labels == "neutral")
cells <- c(which.max(h$fhat), neutral[which.max(h$fhat[neutral])], which.min(h$fhat))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 7, 1, 1))
xr <- range(h$null[cells, ], h$fhat[cells])
plot(NA, xlim = xr, ylim = c(0.5, 3.5), yaxt = "n", xlab = "f-hat", ylab = "")
axis(2, at = 3:1, labels = paste("cell", cells, "\n", h$labels[cells]), las = 1, tick = FALSE)
for (j in 1:3) {
  y0 <- 4 - j
  points(h$null[cells[j], ], jitter(rep(y0, ncol(h$null)), amount = 0.15),
         pch = 16, cex = 0.3, col = "grey70")
  segments(c(h$lower[cells[j]], h$upper[cells[j]]), y0 - 0.3,
           c(h$lower[cells[j]], h$upper[cells[j]]), y0 + 0.3, lwd = 2)
  points(h$fhat[cells[j]], y0, pch = 18, cex = 2,
         col = c(hot = "#e34948", neutral = "grey40", cold = "#2a78d6")[as.character(h$labels[cells[j]])])
}
par(op)
```

The grey points are the 999 permuted fits, the vertical bars the 5% and 95%
quantiles, and the diamond the observed \(\hat f_i\). The middle cell has a positive
\(\hat f_i\) that noise could produce, so it is labelled neutral.

The band is pointwise: when there is no spatial structure, each cell has a 5% chance
of being labelled hot. The test of Step 1 protects the map as a whole, because the
band is only computed when the test rejects.

## Hot and cold cells

```{r labels, fig.height = 3.6}
lab_num <- c(cold = 1, neutral = 2, hot = 3)[as.character(h$labels)]
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
draw_map(lab_num, c("#2a78d6", "#f0efec", "#e34948"), c(1, 3), main = "hot (red) and cold (blue) cells")
zones <- ifelse(is.na(h$zones$hot), 0, h$zones$hot)
draw_map(zones, c("#f0efec", hcl.colors(max(zones), "Set 2")), main = "hot zones")
par(op)
table(h$labels)
```

Since the data are simulated, we know the truth and can check the labels.

```{r check}
hot  <- which(h$labels == "hot")
cold <- which(h$labels == "cold")
c(hot_cells_in_a_cluster   = mean(hot %in% s$footprint),
  cluster_cells_found      = mean(s$footprint %in% hot),
  cold_cells_in_cold_area  = mean(cold %in% s$cold_cells),
  cold_area_found          = mean(s$cold_cells %in% cold),
  hot_cells_in_covariate_area = mean(hot %in% s$cov_cells))
```

`r sum(hot %in% s$cov_cells)` of the `r length(hot)` hot cells are in the covariate area.

## Priority list

When resources only allow treating `m` cells, `rank_cells()` orders the cells: hot
cells first, by decreasing \(\hat f_i\), then the others.

```{r rank}
top <- rank_cells(h)[1:20]
top
mean(top %in% s$footprint)                     # share of the top 20 inside a cluster
mean(order(-s$Y)[1:20] %in% s$footprint)       # the same for the 20 largest counts
```

Ranking by counts mostly picks the covariate area.

## Comparison with Getis-Ord Gi*

The test of Step 1 can be placed in front of any local statistic. Here \(G_i^*\) is
computed on the same residuals of \(\log(1 + Y)\) on the covariates.

```{r gistar}
y <- as.numeric(scale(log1p(s$Y)))
X <- cbind(1, scale(s$Z))
u <- lm.fit(X, y)$residuals
moran_resid(u, s$A, X)$z                       # the z0 of Step 1
gi <- local_gi_star(u, s$A)
gi_hot <- which(gi > qnorm(0.95))
c(gi_hot_cells = length(gi_hot), in_a_cluster = mean(gi_hot %in% s$footprint))
```

\(G_i^*\) labels `r length(gi_hot)` cells hot, `r round(100 * mean(gi_hot %in% s$footprint))`% of
them inside a cluster, against `r round(100 * mean(hot %in% s$footprint))`% for
`hot_cold_map()`. Section 3 of the paper compares the two methods over many simulated
datasets: they perform similarly with strong clusters, `hot_cold_map()` finds clusters of
different sizes more often, and \(G_i^*\) is more precise with weak compact clusters.

## Using your own data

For areal data stored as polygons, the contiguity matrix can be built with the
`spdep` package, and the counts and covariates are columns of the same table:

```{r own-data, eval = FALSE}
library(sf)
library(spdep)
areas <- st_read("my_areas.gpkg")                  # one row per area
A <- nb2mat(poly2nb(areas, queen = TRUE), style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
h <- hot_cold_map(areas$count, st_drop_geometry(areas)[, c("cov1", "cov2")], A)
areas$label <- h$labels
plot(areas["label"])
```

Areas without neighbours should be removed first, because the contiguity matrix
must have at least one neighbour per area for the eigenvectors to be meaningful.
